In one sense, the child reunited his parents. At his little cradle they met in shared hope, shared joy, and shared fear. Both thought about him and talked about him with equal frequency and eagerness; each felt grateful to the other for the child and for all the love and happiness he brought them.
And yet a great distance still separated them.

Lyhne devoted himself entirely to the farm and parish business. He did not set out to lead anyone, or even to bring about reform. Instead, he paid conscientious attention to things as they stood, watched with interest, and introduced the cautious improvements his old head servant or the parish elders recommended after careful—very careful—reflection.

Using the knowledge he had gained in his earlier life never entered his mind. He had too little confidence in what he called theories, and far too much reverence for the venerable, time-sanctioned doctrines of experience that others called practical. In fact, nothing suggested that he had not spent his whole life here, living in precisely this way—except one small habit. For half an hour at a stretch he would sit motionless on a stile or boundary stone, gazing across the lush green rye or the golden, heavy-headed oats, lost in a strange, almost plantlike trance. That belonged to the former Lyhne, the young Lyhne.

In her own world, Bartholine was not nearly so willing to adjust promptly and gracefully. First she had to give her sorrow a voice in the verses of a hundred poets, deploring, in all the sweeping phrases of the age, the countless barriers and chains that weighed on humanity. Sometimes her complaint assumed a tone of noble outrage, hurling its froth of words at emperors' thrones and tyrants' dungeons. Sometimes it became a quiet, compassionate grief, watching beauty's brilliant light drain from a blind, servile generation, frightened and broken by the soulless bustle of modern life. At other times it dwindled to a soft sigh for the freedom of a bird in flight or a cloud floating lightly away.

Eventually she tired of lamentation, and the helplessness of her sorrow drove her towards doubt and bitterness. Like worshippers who strike their saint and trample him when he refuses to display his power, she mocked the romance she had once adored. Scornfully she asked herself whether she expected the bird Roc to turn up in the cucumber bed, or Aladdin's cave to open beneath the milk-cellar floor. She replied with a kind of childish cynicism, insisting that everything in the world was hopelessly ordinary: the moon was green cheese, roses merely potpourri. All this gave her the satisfaction of revenge, mingled with an uneasy, fascinated feeling that she was uttering blasphemies.

These efforts to free herself came to nothing. She returned to her girlhood dreams, but now hope no longer lit them. She also knew what they were: only dreams, remote and deceptive, which no amount of longing could ever bring down to her earth. Giving herself over to them now made her weary. An accusing voice within compared her to a drunkard who knows his craving is destroying him, that every bout of drinking takes strength from his already weakened self and gives it to his desire. The warning was useless. A sober existence without the beautiful vice of dreaming was no existence at all. Life had precisely the worth her dreams bestowed on it, and nothing beyond that.

Such were the differences between Niels Lyhne's mother and father: two benevolent powers unconsciously competing for possession of his young soul from the first glimmer of understanding that gave them something to influence. As he grew, their struggle intensified and its weapons became more varied.

His mother sought to reach him through his imagination. He had imagination in abundance, yet even as a very small boy he plainly distinguished the fairy world her words evoked from the world that actually existed. Often, as she told a story, the hero's troubles would grow so desperate that Niels could see no escape. Misery seemed to close around both the hero and himself like an unbreakable wall, drawing tighter and tighter, and he could not imagine how it could be overcome. More than eleven times, at such a moment, he suddenly laid his cheek against his mother's and whispered, with trembling lips and tear-filled eyes, “But it isn't _really_ true?” Once he had the reassuring answer he wanted, he released a deep sigh and settled contentedly to hear the ending.
This desertion did not altogether please his mother.

Once he outgrew fairy tales and she grew tired of inventing them, she turned to accounts of heroes in war and peace, adding flourishes of her own. She selected figures whose lives could illustrate the strength within a human soul that wills only one thing: a soul neither discouraged by the moment's shortsighted doubts nor tempted into a comfortable peace that saps its energy.

Every story followed that pattern. When history ran out of heroes to her liking, she invented one whose actions and destiny she could fashion at will. He was a hero made to satisfy her own heart, spirit of her spirit—yes, and her own flesh and blood as well.

A few years after Niels's birth she had delivered a stillborn boy, and this was the child she chose. She spread before his brother everything he might have become and accomplished: a confused mixture of Promethean yearning, Messianic courage, and Herculean strength. It was a naïve parody, a monstrous distortion, a whole world of cheap fantasies with no more substance in reality than the tiny skeleton crumbling in the earth of Lönborg graveyard.

Niels understood perfectly what all these stories were meant to teach him. Being like ordinary people was contemptible, and he readily accepted the hard destiny of a hero. In his imagination he willingly endured exhausting struggles, misfortune, the martyrdom of being misunderstood, and victories that brought no peace. Yet alongside this willingness came a wonderful relief: it was all so far away. None of these things would happen until he was grown.

The shapes and sounds of a night's dreaming sometimes stray into the waking day as misty forms, faint shadows of voices. They call to the mind and hold it briefly, listening and wondering whether anyone has really spoken. So the images of that future born of dreams passed whispering through Niels Lyhne's childhood. Gently but incessantly they reminded him that this happy time had a limit, and that one day, before long, it would be gone.

Knowing this made him hunger to experience childhood fully, to drink it in with every sense and spill not one drop, not a single one. His play therefore became intense, sometimes almost frenzied. Behind it lay the uneasy feeling that time was flowing away before he could take everything its treasure-filled waters offered, as one wave broke against the next. Sometimes, when a holiday dragged because he lacked playmates, ideas, or fine weather, he flung himself on the ground and sobbed in despair. He hated bedtime, because sleep contained neither happenings nor sensations.
But he did not always feel that way.

At times he became tired, and the colours drained from his imagination. Then he felt miserable, too small and unimportant for such grand dreams. He saw himself as a contemptible liar, brazenly claiming to understand and love greatness when in truth he cared only for little things and loved only the commonplace. Every low-born wish and appetite lived vigorously inside him. Sometimes he even seemed to feel the rabble's class hatred of everything noble. He could have gladly joined in stoning those heroes, whose blood was finer than his and who knew it.

On those days he avoided his mother. Feeling that he was yielding to an unworthy impulse, he went to his father, ready to listen and open his mind to those earthbound thoughts and matter-of-fact explanations. With his father he felt at home and delighted in their resemblance. He almost forgot that this was the very man he usually regarded with pity from the highest towers of his castle of dreams. Naturally, none of this existed in the child's mind as clearly and distinctly as words make it appear. Yet it was all there, unborn and unshaped, a vague, elusive embryo of feeling. It resembled the strange growth on the seabed as seen through layers of ice. Break that ice, or lift what lives in the dimness into the full light of language: the result is the same. The thing now clearly seen and understood is no longer the shadowy thing it was before.
